responseText: {"galleries":[{"id":"nnotb--mouths-and-teeth","title":"Teeth and Expression","question":"When the same white-marks-against-dark-gap appears in twenty-three heads, what stops it from reading the same way twice?","introduction":"Twenty-three heads, each built around an open mouth. Some bare teeth in tight rows; others spread them wide across a dark void. Some surround them with spirals and zigzags; others with flat color or scribbled lines. Moving through the gallery, watch how the same raw material — white marks against a dark gap — shifts between a grin, a grimace, a shout, and something that fits none of those categories.","closing":"The tooth row reappears in every work, drawn differently each time. Whether any single construction settles into one readable expression is a question the works leave open.","chapters":[{"title":"The Mouth as Structural Center","introduction":"Four works where the open mouth is the feature that draws the eye first and organizes everything else around it — other marks read as secondary to that central gap."},{"title":"Teeth Inside a Decorated Field","introduction":"Five works where the mouth competes with dense borders, zigzag lines, and repeating ornamental marks — the tooth row present but carrying equal visual weight with its surroundings."},{"title":"Grounds That Change the Reading","introduction":"Six works where the background color — amber, yellow, blue, ochre-teal, or teal-green — alters how the mouth and teeth register against it, shifting the same tooth form each time."},{"title":"Two Faces, One Field","introduction":"Four works where a second face, eye, or mouth form shares the composition — the tooth row doubled or placed alongside another presence within the same picture boundary."},{"title":"Layered Marks and the Unresolved Face","introduction":"Five works where accumulated marks, scribbled lines, and color patches build up across the surface so densely that the mouth is the last feature to become readable, if it does at all."}]},{"id":"nnotb--heads-in-darkness","title":"Marks Against Dark","question":"Which specific marks — outline, color band, crossed circle, bare tooth — are enough to hold a face together against a dark ground?","introduction":"Fifteen works share one condition: a dark field that could absorb any form placed against it. Some faces push forward through thick outline; others dissolve into the ground they occupy. Moving through the gallery, you can watch which marks hold a face together — line, color band, crossed circle, bare tooth — and the moments when those marks stop being sufficient.","closing":"Each work returns to the same problem: a dark ground and a set of marks trying to keep a face in place. Whether they fully manage it, or only partly, is a question each image leaves open.","chapters":[{"title":"Outline Holds the Face","introduction":"Three works where a strong outer contour is the primary reason a face or figure stays readable against its dark surround — and where that contour begins to stretch or break."},{"title":"Color Bands Cut Across","introduction":"Four works where a horizontal bar or broad color zone slices through the face, becoming the single mark that most clearly locates a head within the dark field."},{"title":"Crossed Marks and Mismatched Eyes","introduction":"Four works where X-marks, asymmetric eyes, or a split-face division are the visible device that gives each face its distinct character against the surrounding dark."},{"title":"Enclosing Forms","introduction":"Three works where the face sits inside a curved or hooded boundary, raising the question of how much of the face that enclosure actually brings forward versus conceals."},{"title":"When the Ground Wins","introduction":"Two works where the dark field or a competing surround overwhelms the face, leaving marks that suggest a head is present without fully delivering one — or abandoning the face altogether."}]},{"id":"nnotb--blocks-and-volume","title":"Building the Head","question":"What gives a drawn head its structure — and where does that structure leave gaps it cannot close?","introduction":"Fifteen works ask the same question through different means: rectangles stacked in compartments, spirals coiled inside eye sockets, loose lines that escape their outlines, and color patches sitting beneath scaffolding rather than filling it. Move through five chapters and watch how each work decides where one part of the head ends and another begins.","closing":"Each work answers differently — through locked panels, lines that escape their boundaries, or a hollow where a feature should be. The question of what holds a head together stays open.","chapters":[{"title":"Flat Fields and Nested Frames","introduction":"Three works that build faces from zones of flat color and nested rectangles, treating the head as a system of contained compartments rather than a rounded or modeled form."},{"title":"The Segmented Figure","introduction":"Three works where structure extends from face to full body, with plated torsos and blocky heads that treat the whole figure as an assembly of interlocking parts."},{"title":"Lines That Cross the Face","introduction":"Three works that keep the face frontal and close-cropped but run lines across it that do not follow the underlying structure, making the boundary between inside and outside uncertain."},{"title":"Faces as Display Boards","introduction":"Three works that replace expected facial anatomy with panels, grids, and emblems — arrangements that invite the eye to scan across the surface rather than settle on a single focal point."},{"title":"Scaffolding and What It Leaves Open","introduction":"One work closes the gallery: a rounded head where heavy black outlines hold color patches in place but leave a hollow eye socket and an open hatched mouth that the structure does not close."}]}]}
